title: How to verify a marketplace seller
summary: A seller application is a set of claims about who the seller is and what they sell. How to check each one against evidence the seller did not write, at…
body_markdown:
Treat the application as a set of claims and check each one against evidence the seller did not write. Confirm that the person or business is real and consistent, including a registry record for a business, then find the seller's track record on other marketplaces, social shops, websites and forums, and ask them to prove they control it. Check that the stock, prices and volume fit that history, and check again whenever the account's contact details, location, category or volume change.


Look at how long the seller has been on the marketplace, what they have sold before and what buyers said, and search their name with the words complaint or scam, as the FTC suggests. Be careful with expensive brand-name items at bargain prices, which the FTC warns could be counterfeit or stolen. Pay through the marketplace or by credit card, and do not buy from a seller who insists on gift cards, wire transfers, payment apps or cryptocurrency.


An individual is checked mainly through the age and consistency of their name, contact details, location and selling history. A business adds a registry record: look it up where it says it was formed and compare its legal name, formation date and the people named with the application. A registry entry shows that the business was formed, so its track record is what shows that it trades.


Check the claim against the brand's own list of authorised dealers or its store locator, using the current copy, because lists change. Nikon, for example, publishes a dated list of its authorised US dealers. If a brand publishes no list, ask the brand, and keep in mind that a seller missing from a list may still sell genuine goods, so the check tests only the claim of authorisation.


Whenever something checked at onboarding changes: new contact details, a new location or shipping origin, a new name or handle, a sudden change of category or volume, or an old account that wakes up with high-value listings. Social media accounts with a history are bought and sold, and a takeover keeps the history while changing who controls it. Re-run the checks on whatever changed and confirm the change through a contact detail you already hold.


Parts of it can. Reviews can be faked, social media accounts with followers are sold on account marketplaces, and a real person's identity and history can be borrowed. A record built over years by other people is the hardest part to fake, so ask the seller to prove they control each profile they name, and look for changes around the time an account may have changed hands.
